metadata.title: Well Posedness of the Problem of Estimation Fractional Derivative for a Distribution Function.

nodes.name: Nonparametric estimation of the fractional derivative of a distribution function
nodes.statement: {\bf We consider here the problem of the nonparametric estimation of the fractional derivative for a distribution function based on the sample of a "great" volume, and analogously estimation of the fractional derivative of the spectral function of Gaussian stationary sequence. }
nodes.statement_short: Estimate nonparametrically the fractional derivative of a distribution function (and of the spectral function of a Gaussian stationary sequence) from a large sample.

nodes.name: Well-posedness for order alpha < 1/2
nodes.statement: We will prove that if the order of the fractional derivative $ \alpha $ is less than 1/2, then these problems are well posed.
assumptions: if the order of the fractional derivative $ \alpha $ is less than 1/2
conclusions: these problems are well posed
nodes.statement_short: For fractional order $\alpha<1/2$ the estimation problems are well posed.

nodes.name: Sample of volume n
nodes.statement: Let $ \xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots, \xi_n $ be a sample of a volume $ n, $ i.e. independent identical distributed numerical random variable with common distribution function $ F = F(x). $
nodes.genus: independent identical distributed numerical random variable
differentia: with common distribution function $ F = F(x). $

nodes.name: Class K of distributions
nodes.statement: In what follows we restrict ourselves by consideration of the following class $ K $ of distributions: $$ \forall F \in K \ \Rightarrow \exists (a,b) \in R^2, \ 0 \le a < b \le \infty, \ F(a+0) = 0, F(b-0) = 1, $$ such that on the interval $ (a,b) $ the function $ F(x) $ is continuous and strictly increasing.
nodes.statement_short: K: distributions supported on an interval (a,b) on which F is continuous and strictly increasing.

nodes.name: Left endpoint a = 0
nodes.statement: We can and will suppose further without loss of generality $ a = 0. $

nodes.name: Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative
nodes.statement: Let $ \alpha = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in (0,1); $ and let $ g = g(x), \ x \in R $ be measurable numerical function. The fractional derivative of a Rieman-Liouville type of order $ \alpha: \ D^{\alpha}[g](x) = g^{(\alpha)}(x) $ is defined as follows: $ \Gamma(1-\alpha) g^{(\alpha)}(x) = $ $$ \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ D^{\alpha}[g](x) = \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x[g](x) \stackrel{def}{= } \frac{d}{dx} \int_0^x \frac{g(t) \ dt}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}. \eqno(1.1) $$ see, e.g. the classical monograph of S.G.Samko, A.A.Kilbas and O.I.Marichev \cite{Samko1}, pp. 33-38; see also \cite{Miller1}.
nodes.definiendum: fractional derivative of a Rieman-Liouville type of order $ \alpha $
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Liouville derivative: $\Gamma(1-\alpha)D^\alpha[g](x)=\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x g(t)(x-t)^{-\alpha}dt$.

nodes.name: Riemann-Liouville derivative formula (1.1)
nodes.statement: $$ \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ D^{\alpha}[g](x) = \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x[g](x) \stackrel{def}{= } \frac{d}{dx} \int_0^x \frac{g(t) \ dt}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}. \eqno(1.1) $$

nodes.name: Gamma function
nodes.statement: Hereafter $ \Gamma(\cdot) $ denotes the ordinary $ \Gamma \ $ function.

nodes.name: Convention for nonexistent fractional derivative
nodes.statement: We agree to take $ D^{\alpha}[g](x_0) = 0, $ if at the point $ x_0 $ the expression $ D^{\alpha}[g](x_0) $ does not exists.

nodes.name: Non-locality of the fractional derivative
nodes.statement: Notice that the operator of the fractional derivative is non - local, if $ \alpha $ is not integer non-negative number.

nodes.name: Riemann-Liouville fractional integral
nodes.statement: Recall also that the fractional integral $ I^{(\alpha)}[\phi](x) = I^{\alpha}[\phi](x) $ of a Rieman - Liouville type of an order $ \alpha, 0 < \alpha < 1 $ is defined as follows: $$ I^{(\alpha)}[\phi](x) \stackrel{def}{=} \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \cdot \int_0^x \frac{\phi(t) \ dt}{(x-t)^{1 - \alpha}}, \ x,t > 0. \eqno(1.1a) $$
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Liouville fractional integral $I^\alpha[\phi](x)=\Gamma(\alpha)^{-1}\int_0^x\phi(t)(x-t)^{\alpha-1}dt$.

nodes.name: Abel's theorem
nodes.statement: It is known (theorem of Abel, see \cite{Samko1}, chapter 2, section 2.1) that the operator $ I^{(\alpha)}[\cdot] $ is inverse to the fractional derivative operator $ D^{(\alpha)}[\cdot], $ at least in the class of absolutely continuous functions.
assumptions: at least in the class of absolutely continuous functions
conclusions: the operator $ I^{(\alpha)}[\cdot] $ is inverse to the fractional derivative operator $ D^{(\alpha)}[\cdot], $
nodes.statement_short: The fractional integral inverts the fractional derivative on absolutely continuous functions.

nodes.name: Almost-everywhere existence of the fractional derivative
nodes.statement: Note that for the considered further functions this fractional derivative there exists almost everywhere.

nodes.name: Fractional derivative and integral of a step function
nodes.statement: Let us consider the following important example. Define the function $$ g_h(x) = I(h < x), \ x > 0, \ h = \mathop{\rm const}\limits > 0. $$ We conclude after simple calculations taking into account our agreement $$ g_h^{(\alpha)}(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \cdot I(h < x) \cdot (x - h)^{-\alpha}, \ \alpha = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in (0,1). $$ Let us calculate for the verification the fractional integral $ I^{\alpha} $ of order $ \alpha $ from the function $ x \to g_h^{(\alpha)}(\cdot). $ We have $$ \Gamma(\alpha) \Gamma(1 - \alpha) I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = 0, \ x \le h, $$ and in the case $ x > h $ $$ \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = \int_0^x \frac{I(t > h) \ (t - h)^{-\alpha} \ dt}{ (x - t)^{1 - \alpha}} = $$ $$ \int_h^x (t-h)^{-\alpha} \ (x - t)^{\alpha - 1} \ dt. $$ We make the substitution $$ t = h + y(x-h); \hspace{6mm} dt = (x-h) dy: $$ $$ \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = \int_0^1 y^{ - \alpha} \ (1 - y)^{\alpha - 1} \ dy = $$ $$ B(1 - \alpha, \alpha) = \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) / \Gamma(1) = \Gamma(\alpha) \ \Gamma(1 - \alpha), $$ where $ B(\cdot, \cdot) $ denotes the usually Beta function. \par Thus, $$ I^{\alpha} \left[ g_h^{(\alpha)} \right] (x) = I(h < x) = g_h(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: For $g_h=I(h<x)$, $g_h^{(\alpha)}=I(h<x)(x-h)^{-\alpha}/\Gamma(1-\alpha)$ and $I^\alpha$ recovers $g_h$ via a Beta integral.

nodes.name: Example not covered by Abel's theorem
nodes.statement: Note that since the function $ x \to g_h(x) $ is not absolutely continuous, this result can not be obtained from the results of chapter 2 from the monograph \cite{Samko1}.

nodes.name: Loss functional for estimating D^alpha F
nodes.statement: Further, we define as the capacity of a loss function the following $ L_q(R, dF) $ functional $$ \tilde{W}_{n,q} [ D^{\alpha}[F](\cdot), \tilde{F}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[F](x) - \tilde{F}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(1.2) $$ where $ q = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \ge 1, \ \tilde{F}_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is arbitrary estimation of $ D^{\alpha}[F](\cdot) $ based on our sample.
nodes.statement_short: $L_q(dF)$ risk, scaled by $\sqrt n$, of an estimate of $D^\alpha[F]$.

nodes.name: Reliability function and loss functional W_{n,q}
nodes.statement: But it is more convenient sometimes to consider the equivalent problem of estimation of the fractional derivative of so-called "reliability" function $ D^{\alpha}[G](x), $ where $$ G(x) = {\bf P} (\xi_i \ge x) = 1 - F(x), \eqno(1.3) $$ and to take $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) = D^{\alpha}G(x), $ $$ W_{n,q} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(1.4) $$ where in turn $ \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is arbitrary estimation of $ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) $ based on our sample.
nodes.statement_short: Reliability function $G=1-F$, its fractional derivative $G^{(\alpha)}$, and the $\sqrt n$-scaled $L_q(dF)$ risk $W_{n,q}$ of an estimate of it.

nodes.name: Loss functional W_{n,q} (1.4)
nodes.statement: $$ W_{n,q} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(1.4) $$

nodes.name: Fractional derivative of the constant and relation (1.4a)
nodes.statement: Note that $$ D^{\alpha}[1](x) = \frac{x^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha) } \ne 0, $$ so that $$ D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{x^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha) } - D^{\alpha}[F](x) \ne - D^{\alpha}[F](x). \eqno(1.4a) $$
conclusions: $$ D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{x^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha) } - D^{\alpha}[F](x) \ne - D^{\alpha}[F](x). \eqno(1.4a) $$
nodes.statement_short: $D^\alpha[1](x)=x^{-\alpha}/\Gamma(1-\alpha)$, so $D^\alpha[G]=x^{-\alpha}/\Gamma(1-\alpha)-D^\alpha[F]$.

nodes.name: Relation between D^alpha G and D^alpha F (1.4a)
nodes.statement: $$ D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{x^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha) } - D^{\alpha}[F](x) \ne - D^{\alpha}[F](x). \eqno(1.4a) $$

nodes.name: Empirical approximation of the loss
nodes.statement: For the practical using the expression (1.4) may be consistent approximate as $ n \to \infty $ as follows $$ W_q [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \approx \sqrt{n} \times \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - \tilde{G}_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF_n(x) \right]^{1/q}, $$ where $ F_n(x) $ is ordinary empirical function of distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $dF$ by the empirical distribution $dF_n$ to approximate the loss (1.4) for large n.

nodes.name: Empirical reliability function
nodes.statement: We can define analogously the following estimate of the function $ G(x): $ $$ G_n(x) := n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n I(\xi_i \ge x), \eqno(1.5) $$ empirical reliability function.

nodes.name: Indicator function
nodes.statement: Here $ I(\xi_i \ge x) $ is the usually indicator function: $$ I(\xi_i \ge x) = 1 \ \Leftrightarrow \xi_i \ge x; \hspace{6mm} I(\xi_i \ge x) = 0 \ \Leftrightarrow \xi_i < x. $$

nodes.name: Kolmogorov's theorem
nodes.statement: Evidently, (Kolmogorov's theorem), the problem of distribution function estimation $ (\alpha = 0) $ is well posed.
conclusions: the problem of distribution function estimation $ (\alpha = 0) $ is well posed

nodes.name: Konakov's ill-posedness of density estimation
nodes.statement: V.D.Konakov in \cite{Konakov1} proved in contradiction that the problem of density estimation, i.e. when $ \alpha = 1, $ is ill posed.
conclusions: the problem of density estimation, i.e. when $ \alpha = 1, $ is ill posed

nodes.name: Well-posed statistical estimation problem
nodes.statement: Certain problem of statistical estimation is well posed iff there exists an estimate (more exactly, a sequence of estimates) such that the speed of convergence is equal (or less than) $ 1/\sqrt{n}. $
differentia: there exists an estimate (more exactly, a sequence of estimates) such that the speed of convergence is equal (or less than) $ 1/\sqrt{n}. $

nodes.name: Standing assumptions of Section 2
nodes.statement: {\bf 0.} {\it We suppose in what follows in this section that $ x > 0 $ and } $ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, $ so that $ a = 0, \ 0 < b \le \infty. $

nodes.name: Step function f_h
nodes.statement: {\bf 1.} Let us consider the following function $$ x \to f_h(x) = I(x < h), \ h = \mathop{\rm const}\limits > 0. \eqno(2.1) $$

nodes.name: Kernel f_{alpha,h}
nodes.statement: It is easy to calculate that $$ f_{\alpha,h}(x) := \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ D^{\alpha}[f_h](x) = x^{-\alpha} - (x - h)^{-\alpha} \cdot I(x > h), \ x > 0. \eqno(2.2) $$
nodes.statement_short: $f_{\alpha,h}(x)=\Gamma(1-\alpha)D^\alpha[f_h](x)=x^{-\alpha}-(x-h)^{-\alpha}I(x>h)$.

nodes.name: Estimate G_{alpha,n} of the fractional derivative of G
nodes.statement: {\bf 2.} It is reasonable to offer as a capacity of the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ at the fixed point $ x, \ x > 0 $ of the fractional derivative $ D^{\alpha}[G](x) $ the following statistic: $$ \Gamma(1-\alpha) \cdot G_{\alpha,n}(x) \stackrel{def}{=} n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x). \eqno(2.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: Point estimate: $\Gamma(1-\alpha)G_{\alpha,n}(x)$ is the sample mean of $f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x)$.

nodes.name: Variance function Sigma^2_alpha
nodes.statement: Denote also $$ \Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x) := 2x^{-\alpha} \Gamma(1 - \alpha) G^{(\alpha)}(x) - \Gamma(1 - 2 \alpha) \ G^{(2 \alpha)}(x) - \left(\Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right)^2. \eqno(2.4) $$

nodes.name: Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: {\bf 3. \ Theorem 2.1.} \\ {\bf A.} Suppose that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) $ there exists. Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is not biased: $$ {\bf E} G_{\alpha,n}(x) = G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.5) $$ \vspace{3mm} {\bf B.} Suppose in addition that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(2 \alpha)}(x) $ there exists. Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is asymptotically as $ n \to \infty $ normal with the variance $$ \mathop{\rm Var}\limits \left[ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right] = \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)}: \eqno(2.6) $$ \vspace{3mm} $$ \mathop{\rm Law}\limits \left\{ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right\} \sim N \left(G^{(\alpha)}(x), \ \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)} \right). \eqno(2.7) $$
assumptions: Suppose that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) $ there exists.
Suppose in addition that at the fixed positive point $ x $ the fractional derivative $ G^{(2 \alpha)}(x) $ there exists.
conclusions: Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is not biased:
$$ {\bf E} G_{\alpha,n}(x) = G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.5) $$
Then the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is asymptotically as $ n \to \infty $ normal with the variance
$$ \mathop{\rm Law}\limits \left\{ G_{\alpha,n}(x) \right\} \sim N \left(G^{(\alpha)}(x), \ \frac{\Sigma^2_{\alpha}(x)}{n \ \Gamma^2(1 - \alpha)} \right). \eqno(2.7) $$
nodes.statement_short: The point estimate $G_{\alpha,n}(x)$ is unbiased and, if $G^{(2\alpha)}(x)$ exists, asymptotically normal with variance $\Sigma^2_\alpha(x)/(n\Gamma^2(1-\alpha))$.

nodes.name: Unbiasedness (2.5)
nodes.statement: $$ {\bf E} G_{\alpha,n}(x) = G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.5) $$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} It is sufficient to prove the equality (2.5) only for the value $ n = 1. $ We deduce by direct computation using the source definition (1.1) $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot D^{\alpha}_x I(\xi \ge x) \ = \ x^{-\alpha} - (x-\xi)^{-\alpha} \cdot I(\xi < x)= $$ $$ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x), \hspace{6mm} \xi = \xi_1. \eqno(2.8) $$ It remains to take the expectation $ {\bf E} $ from both the sides of the relationship (2.8) to establish the unbiaseness. \par Let us calculate the variance; we consider of course the case $ n = 1. $ $$ \mathop{\rm Var}\limits := \mathop{\rm Var}\limits \left[ x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = $$ $$ \mathop{\rm Var}\limits \left[ (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = S_2 - S_1^2, \eqno(2.9) $$ where $$ S_1 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} \ I(\xi < x) $$ and we know that $$ S_1 = x^{-\alpha} - \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.10) $$ Further, we will use the formula (2.24), section 2, pp. 35-37 from the book \cite{Samko1}: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x [F] = \frac{F(0)}{x^{\alpha}} + \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}} = \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}, $$ since $ F(0) = F(0+) = 0. $ Therefore $$ S_2 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-2 \alpha} \ I(\xi < x) = \int_0^x \frac{d F(t)}{(x-t)^{2 \alpha}} = \Gamma(1 - 2 \alpha) \ D^{2 \alpha}[F](x). \eqno(2.11) $$ It remains to substitute into equality (2.9), taking into account the relation (1.4a). \par The asymptotical normality our estimate follows now from the classical one-dimensional CLT.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation for n=1: $\Gamma(1-\alpha)D^\alpha I(\xi\ge x)=f_{\alpha,\xi}(x)$ gives unbiasedness; variance via Samko's formula for $D^{2\alpha}$, normality by the classical CLT.

nodes.name: Kernel identity (2.8)
nodes.statement: $$ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x), \hspace{6mm} \xi = \xi_1. \eqno(2.8) $$

nodes.name: Variance decomposition (2.9)
nodes.statement: $$ \mathop{\rm Var}\limits \left[ (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = S_2 - S_1^2, \eqno(2.9) $$

nodes.name: Reduce to n = 1
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} It is sufficient to prove the equality (2.5) only for the value $ n = 1. $
nodes.statement_short: Reduce unbiasedness to a single observation.

nodes.name: Kernel identity
nodes.statement: We deduce by direct computation using the source definition (1.1) $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot D^{\alpha}_x I(\xi \ge x) \ = \ x^{-\alpha} - (x-\xi)^{-\alpha} \cdot I(\xi < x)= $$ $$ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x), \hspace{6mm} \xi = \xi_1. \eqno(2.8) $$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\Gamma(1-\alpha)D^\alpha I(\xi\ge x)=f_{\alpha,\xi}(x)$ from (1.1).

nodes.name: Take expectations
nodes.statement: It remains to take the expectation $ {\bf E} $ from both the sides of the relationship (2.8) to establish the unbiaseness.
nodes.statement_short: Taking expectation of (2.8) gives unbiasedness.

nodes.name: Variance decomposition
nodes.statement: Let us calculate the variance; we consider of course the case $ n = 1. $ $$ \mathop{\rm Var}\limits := \mathop{\rm Var}\limits \left[ x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = $$ $$ \mathop{\rm Var}\limits \left[ (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} I(\xi < x) \right] = S_2 - S_1^2, \eqno(2.9) $$ where $$ S_1 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-\alpha} \ I(\xi < x) $$ and we know that $$ S_1 = x^{-\alpha} - \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ G^{(\alpha)}(x). \eqno(2.10) $$
nodes.statement_short: Write the variance as $S_2-S_1^2$ with $S_1$ known.

nodes.name: Recall Samko formula
nodes.statement: Further, we will use the formula (2.24), section 2, pp. 35-37 from the book \cite{Samko1}: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ D^{\alpha}_x [F] = \frac{F(0)}{x^{\alpha}} + \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}} = \int_0^x \frac{dF(t)}{(x-t)^{\alpha}}, $$ since $ F(0) = F(0+) = 0. $
nodes.statement_short: Recall Samko's formula expressing $D^\alpha[F]$ as a Stieltjes integral.

nodes.name: Compute S_2
nodes.statement: Therefore $$ S_2 = {\bf E} (x - \xi)^{-2 \alpha} \ I(\xi < x) = \int_0^x \frac{d F(t)}{(x-t)^{2 \alpha}} = \Gamma(1 - 2 \alpha) \ D^{2 \alpha}[F](x). \eqno(2.11) $$
nodes.statement_short: Express $S_2$ through $D^{2\alpha}[F]$.

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement: It remains to substitute into equality (2.9), taking into account the relation (1.4a).
nodes.statement_short: Substitute into (2.9) using (1.4a).

nodes.name: Apply CLT
nodes.statement: The asymptotical normality our estimate follows now from the classical one-dimensional CLT.
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic normality from the classical CLT.

nodes.name: Remark 2.1 (strong consistency)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.1.} As follows from the relation (2.8), under condition $ |G^{(\alpha)}(x)| < \infty $ the variable $ f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) $ has a finite absolute expectation: $$ {\bf E} |f_{\alpha,\xi} (x)| < \infty. $$ Therefore, on the basis of the Law of Large Numbers, the estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ is consistent with probability one only under the condition $ |G^{(\alpha)}(x)| < \infty. $
nodes.statement_short: If $|G^{(\alpha)}(x)|<\infty$ the summands are integrable, so by the LLN the estimate is strongly consistent.

nodes.name: Remark 2.2 (optimality unknown)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.2.} We are not sure that offered in this report estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(x) $ of the value $ G^{(\alpha)}(x) $ is optimal, in the contradiction to the Kolmogorov's estimate of the ordinary distribution function.

nodes.name: Remark 2.3 (estimating G^{(2alpha)})
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.3.} Emerging in the theorem 2.1 the variable $ G^{( 2 \alpha)}(x), $ which may be used by the practical application, may be consistent estimated as follows: $$ G^{( 2 \alpha)}(x) \approx G_{2 \alpha,n}(x), $$ as long as $ \alpha < 1/2. $

nodes.name: Remark 2.4 (non-asymptotical approach)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 2.4.} Non-asymptotical approach. \par Let $ x $ be fixed positive number; we consider a non-asymptotical deviation $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_n {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \cdot \left| G_{\alpha,n}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right), \ y \ge 3. \eqno(2.12) $$ Note that the summand r.v. $ f_{\alpha,\xi} = x^{-\alpha} - (x - \xi)^{-\alpha}\cdot I(x > \xi) $ has a heavy tail. Namely, if $$ F(x) - F(0) = F(x) \sim C_1 \ x^{\Delta}, \ x \to 0+, \ \Delta = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in (0,1], \ \eqno(2.13) $$ then $$ {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) \sim C_2(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}, \ y \to \infty. \eqno(2.14) $$ The non-asymptotical bounds for $ \sqrt{n} $ normed deviations of sums of these variables are obtained, e.g. the articles \cite{Adler1}, \cite{Bravernan1}, \cite{Bravernan2}, \cite{Ostrovsky3}. We deduce the upper bound for considered probability using these results: $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \le C_3(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha} \ \ln y, \ y > 3. \eqno(2.15) $$ The lower estimate for these probability is trivial: as $ y \to \infty $ $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \ge {\bf P} \left( \left| G_{\alpha,1}(x) - G^{(\alpha)}(x) \right| > y \right) = C_4(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha}(1 + o(1) ). \eqno(2.16) $$ The ultimate value of the degree of the value $ \ln y $ in (2.15) is now unknown.
nodes.statement_short: The summands have heavy tails $\sim y^{-\Delta/\alpha}$ when $F(x)\sim C x^\Delta$ near 0; uniform-in-n tail bounds $\lesssim y^{-\Delta/\alpha}\ln y$ follow from heavy-tail sum results.

nodes.name: Uniform tail bound (2.15)
nodes.statement: $$ P_{\alpha,x}(y) \le C_3(\alpha,x) \cdot y^{-\Delta/\alpha} \ \ln y, \ y > 3. \eqno(2.15) $$

nodes.name: Optimal power of ln y in (2.15)
nodes.statement: The ultimate value of the degree of the value $ \ln y $ in (2.15) is now unknown.

nodes.name: No uniform-norm theory
nodes.statement: As long as the function $ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) $ and correspondingly its estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) $ both are discontinuous and all the more so are unbounded, we can not do the error estimation in the uniform norm, and still can not apply the CLT in the Prokhorov-Skorokhod space, in contradiction to the classical Kolmogorov's theorem.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: Since $D^\alpha[G]$ and its estimate are discontinuous and unbounded, uniform-norm error and CLT in Skorokhod space are unavailable.

nodes.name: L_q(dF) deviation W_{q,n}
nodes.statement: We intent to investigate the $ L_q(dF) $ deviation of empirical derivative reliability function $ G_{\alpha,n} $ from its true value $ D^{\alpha}G: \ W_{q,n} :=$ $$ W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \cdot \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - G_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(3.1) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: L_q deviation (3.1)
nodes.statement: $$ W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \stackrel{def}{=} \sqrt{n} \cdot \left[ {\bf E} \int_R | D^{\alpha}[G](x) - G_{\alpha,n}(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \eqno(3.1) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Distribution-freeness of W_q; reduction to uniform
nodes.statement: Note first of all that the expression for $ W_q $ in (3.1) does not depend on the function $ F(\cdot) $ inside the set $ K = \{ F \}, $ as in the Kolmogorov's theorem; therefore we can and will suppose $ F(x) = x, 0 \le x \le 1, $ i.e. $ a = 0, b = 1 $ and the r.v. $ \{ \xi_i \} $ have the uniform distribution on the set $ [0,1].$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: The loss (3.1) does not depend on $F\in K$, so WLOG the sample is uniform on [0,1].

nodes.name: Covariance R_alpha, normalized process zeta_n and limit Gaussian process
nodes.statement: We introduce some new notations. $ x \cap y := \min(x,y), \ 1 \le q = \mathop{\rm const}\limits < 1/\alpha, $ $$ R_{\alpha}(x,y) \stackrel{def}{=} \frac{( x \cap y )^{1 - 2 \alpha}}{1 - 2 \alpha} \ - \frac{(x \ y)^{1 - \alpha}}{(1 - \alpha)^2}, \ 0 \le x,y < 1, \ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, \eqno(3.2) $$ $$ \sigma^2_{\alpha}(x):= R_{\alpha}(x,x) = \frac{ x^{1 - 2 \alpha}}{1 - 2 \alpha} \ - \frac{x^{2 - 2\alpha}}{(1 - \alpha)^2}, $$ $$ g_{\alpha}(x) = x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha}, $$ \vspace{3mm} $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(x) = \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ \zeta_n(x) := $$ $$ n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left\{ f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x) - \left[ x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} \right] \right\} = $$ $$ n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left\{ f_{\alpha,\xi_i}(x) - g_{\alpha}(x) \right\}, \eqno(3.3) $$ $ \zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x) = \zeta^{(\alpha)}(x) = \zeta(x), \ 0 \le x \le 1 $ be a separable (moreover, continuous with probability one) centered Gaussian random process with covariation function $ R_{\alpha}(x,y): $ \par $$ \mathop{\rm Cov}\limits(\zeta_{\alpha}(x), \zeta_{\alpha}(y)) = {\bf E} \zeta_{\alpha}(x) \cdot \zeta_{\alpha}(y)= R_{\alpha}(x,y). \eqno(3.4) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: Defines covariance $R_\alpha$, variance $\sigma^2_\alpha$, mean $g_\alpha$, the normalized empirical process $\zeta_n^{(\alpha)}$ and the centered Gaussian limit $\zeta^{(\alpha)}$ with covariance $R_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Lebesgue-Riesz space L_q(dF)
nodes.statement: The ordinary Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(dF) = L_q(R_+,dF) $ consists by definition on all the measurable functions $ f: R_+ \to R $ with finite norms $$ ||f||_q = ||f||L_q(dF) \stackrel{def}{=} \left[ \int_0^{\infty} |f(x)|^q \ dF(x) \right]^{1/q}, \ q = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \ge 1. $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Theorem 3.1 (CLT in Lebesgue-Riesz space)
nodes.statement: {\bf Theorem 3.1.} Let $ F(\cdot) \in K $ and let $ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $ Our statement: the sequence of distributions generated in the space $ L_q(dF) $ by the random processes $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ converges weakly as $ n \to \infty $ to the random process $ \zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x) $ (the CLT in the space $ L_q(R_+, dF). $
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
assumptions: Let $ F(\cdot) \in K $ and let $ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $
conclusions: the sequence of distributions generated in the space $ L_q(dF) $ by the random processes $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ converges weakly as $ n \to \infty $ to the random process $ \zeta_{\infty}^{(\alpha)}(x) $
nodes.statement_short: For $1\le q<1/\alpha$, $\zeta_n^{(\alpha)}$ satisfies the CLT in $L_q(dF)$ with Gaussian limit of covariance $R_\alpha$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} Note first of all that here $$ G^{(\alpha)}(x) = D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[ x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} \right]. \eqno(3.5) $$ as long as in this section $ G(x) = 1 - x, \ x \in (0,1). $ Therefore, all the processes $ \zeta_n(x) $ are centered.\par As before, it is sufficient to consider the centered random process $ \zeta_{1}^{(\alpha)}(x), \ x \in (0,1). $ It is easy to calculate its covariation function; it coincides with $ R_{\alpha}(x,y). $ \par It remains to establish the CLT in the Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(0,1) $ for the sequence $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot). $ The using for us version of CLT in this spaces is obtained, for example, in the fundamental monograph \cite{Ledoux1}, pp. 308-319. Namely, the sufficient condition $$ {\bf E} ||\zeta_1||_q^q < \infty \eqno(3.6) $$ is here satisfied, as long as $ q < 1/\alpha. $ \par In detail, let us denote $$ K(\alpha,q) := \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} < \infty, \eqno(3.7) $$ then $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)| \le \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} + (| (x - \xi)|I(x> \xi)|)^{-\alpha}; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)|^q \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + x^{ - \alpha q } \right]; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q^q = \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ \int_0^1|\zeta_1(x)|^q \ dx \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]; $$ so $$ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q \le \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} = K(\alpha,q) < \infty, \eqno(3.7a) $$ since $ 0 < \alpha < 1, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} This completes the proof of theorem 3.1.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to uniform sample, compute covariance $R_\alpha$, and apply the Ledoux-Talagrand CLT in $L_q$ via the deterministic bound $\|\zeta_1\|_q\le K(\alpha,q)$.

nodes.name: Constant K(alpha,q) (3.7)
nodes.statement: $$ K(\alpha,q) := \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} < \infty, \eqno(3.7) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Deterministic norm bound (3.7a)
nodes.statement: $$ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q \le \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} = K(\alpha,q) < \infty, \eqno(3.7a) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Centering
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} Note first of all that here $$ G^{(\alpha)}(x) = D^{\alpha}[G](x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[ x^{-\alpha} - \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} \right]. \eqno(3.5) $$ as long as in this section $ G(x) = 1 - x, \ x \in (0,1). $ Therefore, all the processes $ \zeta_n(x) $ are centered.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $G^{(\alpha)}$ for uniform F; processes are centered.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Reduce to n = 1; covariance
nodes.statement: As before, it is sufficient to consider the centered random process $ \zeta_{1}^{(\alpha)}(x), \ x \in (0,1). $ It is easy to calculate its covariation function; it coincides with $ R_{\alpha}(x,y). $
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $\zeta_1$, whose covariance is $R_\alpha$.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Remaining task
nodes.statement: It remains to establish the CLT in the Lebesgue-Riesz space $ L_q(0,1) $ for the sequence $ \zeta_{n}^{(\alpha)}(\cdot). $
nodes.statement_short: It remains to prove the CLT in $L_q(0,1)$.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Apply Ledoux-Talagrand CLT
nodes.statement: The using for us version of CLT in this spaces is obtained, for example, in the fundamental monograph \cite{Ledoux1}, pp. 308-319. Namely, the sufficient condition $$ {\bf E} ||\zeta_1||_q^q < \infty \eqno(3.6) $$ is here satisfied, as long as $ q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.statement_short: Ledoux-Talagrand sufficient condition $E\|\zeta_1\|_q^q<\infty$ holds for $q<1/\alpha$.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Bound the norm
nodes.statement: In detail, let us denote $$ K(\alpha,q) := \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} < \infty, \eqno(3.7) $$ then $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)| \le \frac{x^{1 - \alpha}}{1 - \alpha} + (| (x - \xi)|I(x> \xi)|)^{-\alpha}; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ |\zeta_1(x)|^q \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + x^{ - \alpha q } \right]; $$ $$ \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q^q = \Gamma^q(1 - \alpha) \ \int_0^1|\zeta_1(x)|^q \ dx \le 2^{q-1} \left[ (1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]; $$ so $$ ||\zeta_1(\cdot)||_q \le \frac{2^{1 - 1/q}}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \cdot \left[(1 - \alpha)^{-q} + (1 - \alpha q)^{-1} \right]^{1/q} = K(\alpha,q) < \infty, \eqno(3.7a) $$ since $ 0 < \alpha < 1, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} This completes the proof of theorem 3.1.
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise bound gives $\|\zeta_1\|_q\le K(\alpha,q)<\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Remark 3.1 (deterministic bound)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.1.} Note that the obtained estimate (3.7a) is deterministic, i.e. is true still without the expectation {\bf E.}
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Remark 3.2 (confidence regions in L_q)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.2.} Let us denote $$ Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) = {\bf P} \left( || \zeta_{\alpha}(\cdot)||L_q(0,1) > u \right), \ u = \mathop{\rm const}\limits > 0. \eqno(3.8) $$ We deduce as a consequence of the theorem 3.1 for the values $ q = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in [1, 1/\alpha),\ \alpha \in (0,1/2) $ and $ u > 0 $ $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) = Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u), \eqno(3.9) $$ therefore for sufficiently greatest values $ n $ $$ {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) \approx Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u). \eqno(3.10) $$ The asymptotical behavior of the probability $ Q_{\alpha}(u) $ as $ u \to \infty $ is known, see \cite{Piterbarg1},\cite{Piterbarg2}. Briefly, let us denote $ q' = q/(q - 1), \ q > 1, $ and introduce the variable $$ \beta := \sup_{h: ||h||L(q') = 1} \left\{ \int_0^1 \int_0^1 R_{\alpha}(x,y) h(x) h(y) dx dy \right\}, $$ which may be computed in turn through solving of some non-linear integral equation; then $$ \ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim - \frac{u^2}{2 \beta^2}, \ u \to \infty. $$ The non-asymptotical estimates of this probability is obtained in \cite{Ostrovsky1}, chapter 4, section 4.8; see also \cite{Ostrovsky2}, chapter 3.\par It is clear that the equality (3.10) may be used by construction of confidence region for the unknown function $ G^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm $ L_q(dF) $ and for the testing of non-parametrical hypotheses.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 gives the limiting law $Q^{(q)}_\alpha$ of the scaled $L_q$ error, whose Gaussian tail is known (Piterbarg-Fatalov), enabling confidence regions and tests.

nodes.name: Tail function Q_alpha^{(q)}
nodes.statement: Let us denote $$ Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) = {\bf P} \left( || \zeta_{\alpha}(\cdot)||L_q(0,1) > u \right), \ u = \mathop{\rm const}\limits > 0. \eqno(3.8) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Limiting law of the L_q error
nodes.statement: We deduce as a consequence of the theorem 3.1 for the values $ q = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in [1, 1/\alpha),\ \alpha \in (0,1/2) $ and $ u > 0 $ $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) = Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u), \eqno(3.9) $$ therefore for sufficiently greatest values $ n $ $$ {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) \approx Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u). \eqno(3.10) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
assumptions: for the values $ q = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in [1, 1/\alpha),\ \alpha \in (0,1/2) $ and $ u > 0 $
conclusions: $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) = Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u), \eqno(3.9) $$
nodes.statement_short: $P(\|G_{\alpha,n}-G^{(\alpha)}\|_{L_q}>u/(\sqrt n\Gamma(1-\alpha)))\to Q^{(q)}_\alpha(u)$.

nodes.name: Large-n approximation (3.10)
nodes.statement: $$ {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) \approx Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u). \eqno(3.10) $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Gaussian norm tail asymptotics (Piterbarg-Fatalov)
nodes.statement: The asymptotical behavior of the probability $ Q_{\alpha}(u) $ as $ u \to \infty $ is known, see \cite{Piterbarg1},\cite{Piterbarg2}. Briefly, let us denote $ q' = q/(q - 1), \ q > 1, $ and introduce the variable $$ \beta := \sup_{h: ||h||L(q') = 1} \left\{ \int_0^1 \int_0^1 R_{\alpha}(x,y) h(x) h(y) dx dy \right\}, $$ which may be computed in turn through solving of some non-linear integral equation; then $$ \ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim - \frac{u^2}{2 \beta^2}, \ u \to \infty. $$
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: $$ \ln Q_{\alpha}^{(q)}(u) \sim - \frac{u^2}{2 \beta^2}, \ u \to \infty. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\ln Q^{(q)}_\alpha(u)\sim -u^2/(2\beta^2)$ with $\beta$ a quadratic-form supremum of $R_\alpha$ over the dual unit ball.

nodes.name: Remark 3.3 (verification at alpha -> 0)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 3.3. Verification.} It is interest to note that on the case $ \alpha = 0, $ more exactly when $ \alpha \to 0+, $ the obtained before results coincide with the classical belonging to Kolmogorov, Mises etc.
nodes.section: 3 Main result: error estimation in Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Uniform-in-n loss and tail probability
nodes.statement: We intent to obtain in this section the non-asymptotical {\it upper} estimate for the supremum of loss function $$ \overline{W}_q \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \eqno(4.0) $$ and as a consequence by means of Tchebychev's inequality the probability $$ \sup_n {\bf P} \left( || G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) - G^{(\alpha)}||L_q(dF) > \frac{u}{\sqrt{n} \Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \right) =: \overline{Q}_{\alpha}(u). \eqno(4.1) $$
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: $\overline W_q=\sup_n W_{q,n}$ and $\overline Q_\alpha(u)$, the sup over n of the scaled $L_q$ error tail.

nodes.name: Standing assumptions of Section 4
nodes.statement: We retain in this section all the notations and restrictions of third section; for instance, $ F(\cdot) \in K; $ therefore we can and will suppose that the r.v. $ \{ \xi(i) \} $ are independent and uniformly distributed on the set $ [0,1]. $
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Kiefer's exponential bound for the empirical distribution function
nodes.statement: The case $ \alpha = 0, $ i.e. when we consider the classical problem of estimation of ordinary distribution function $ F(x) $ or equally the reliability function $ G(x) = 1 - F(x) $ by means of empirical distribution function $ F_n(x), $ is investigated, and at once in the multidimensional case, even in the uniform norm, i.e. when formally $ q = \infty, $ in the work of J.Kiefer \cite{Kiefer1}; more exact estimate see in the article \cite{Gaivoronsky1}. Indeed, $$ {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \sup_{x} |G_n(x) - G(x)|> u \right) \le 2 e^{- 2 u^2}, \ u \ge 1, \eqno(4.2) $$ i.e. the exponential bound for $ \sqrt{n} $ normed uniform deviation $ \sup_{x} |G_n(x) - G(x)|. $
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: $$ {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \sup_{x} |G_n(x) - G(x)|> u \right) \le 2 e^{- 2 u^2}, \ u \ge 1, \eqno(4.2) $$
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha=0$: $P(\sqrt n\sup_x|G_n-G|>u)\le 2e^{-2u^2}$.

nodes.name: No exponential L_p confidence region for p >= 1/alpha
nodes.statement: Note first of all that the $ \sqrt{n} $ exponential tail distributed confidence region for $ G^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ based on our estimate $ G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) $ in the $ L_p $ norm is impossible when $ p \ge 1/\alpha, $ in contradiction to the classical ordinary case $ \alpha = 0. $
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: An exponentially-tailed $\sqrt n$ confidence region in $L_p$ is impossible for $p\ge1/\alpha$.

nodes.name: Lower bound argument
nodes.statement: Namely, we can deduce the following simple {\it lower } bound for $ \overline{W}_q $ $$ \overline{W}_q \ge W_{q,1} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,1}(\cdot) ], $$ and it is easily to calculate analogously to the relations (3.7) - (3.7a) that $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot {\bf E}|| \left[ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) - G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) \right] ||_q \ge \frac{C_1(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q} }, \ q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(4.3) $$ and $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot {\bf E}|| \left[ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot) - G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) \right] ||_q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha, \eqno(4.4) $$
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound by the n=1 term; computing as in (3.7)-(3.7a) shows the expected $L_q$ error blows up like $(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}$ and is infinite for $q\ge1/\alpha$.

nodes.name: 2 <= q < 1/alpha
nodes.statement: We suppose in the sequel $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha. $
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1 (non-asymptotic L_q bound)
nodes.statement: {\bf Theorem 4.1.} We propose under formulated above conditions $ 0 < \alpha < 1/2, \ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha $ etc. $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le \frac{C_2(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q}}, \eqno(4.5) $$ where $ C_2(\alpha) $ is continuous positive function on the closed segment $ \alpha \in [0, 1/2]. $
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
conclusions: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le \frac{C_2(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q}}, \eqno(4.5) $$
nodes.statement_short: Uniformly in n, $\Gamma(1-\alpha)W_{q,n}\le C_2(\alpha)(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}$ for $2\le q<1/\alpha$.

nodes.name: Non-asymptotic bound (4.5)
nodes.statement: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \cdot \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le \frac{C_2(\alpha)}{(1 - \alpha q)^{1/q}}, \eqno(4.5) $$
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} Denote $$ \tau_i(x) = f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x) - {\bf E} f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x), \eqno(4.6) $$ $$ S_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x), \eqno(4.7) $$ then $ \tau_i(x) $ is a sequence of independent identical distributed centered random fields which are proportional with coefficient $ 1/\Gamma(1 - \alpha) $ to the considered before r.f. $ \zeta_i(x). $ \par Let us consider the sequence of random variables $$ V_{\alpha,q}(n) = ||S_n(\cdot)||_q^q = \int_0^1 |S_n(x)|^q \ dx, $$ then we have using Fubini-Tonelli theorem under our condition $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha $ $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) = \int_0^1 {\bf E} |S_n(x)|^q \ dx= \int_0^1 {\bf E} \left| n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x) \right|^q \ dx. \eqno(4.8) $$ We intent to exploit the famous Rosenthal's inequality, see \cite{Rosenthal1}, \cite{Ostrovsky4}. Namely, for arbitrary sequence $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ of independent centered random variables $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot \sqrt{ \sum_{k=1}^n |\zeta_k|_q^2/n }, \hspace{4mm} q \ge 2, \eqno(4.9) $$ where the "Rosenthal's" constant $ K_{R} $ is less than 0.6535, see \cite{Ostrovsky4}. \par If the r.v. $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ are in addition identically distributed, then $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.10) $$ As long as in this section $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha, $ $$ \frac{q}{\ln q} \le \max \left[ \frac{2}{\ln 2}, \ \frac{1/\alpha}{|\ln \alpha|} \right], $$ and if we denote $$ K_{R,\alpha} = K_R \cdot \max \left[ \frac{2}{\ln 2}, \ \frac{1/\alpha}{|\ln \alpha|} \right], \eqno(4.11) $$ then there holds the following inequality (under our conditions) $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R,\alpha} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.12) $$ We conclude after substitution into (4.8) $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) \le K(\alpha,q)^q \cdot K^q_{R,\alpha}. \eqno(4.13) $$ It remains to extract the root of degree $ q $ from last inequality to obtain the estimate $$ \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le K(\alpha,q) \cdot K_{R,\alpha}, $$ which is equivalent to the assertion if theorem 4.1 with explicit evaluate of constant.
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.
nodes.statement_short: Fubini-Tonelli reduces $E\|S_n\|_q^q$ to pointwise moments; Rosenthal's inequality bounds them by $K_{R,\alpha}|\zeta_1|_q$ and (3.7a) gives explicit constant $K(\alpha,q)K_{R,\alpha}$.

nodes.name: Fubini-Tonelli moment identity (4.8)
nodes.statement: $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) = \int_0^1 {\bf E} |S_n(x)|^q \ dx= \int_0^1 {\bf E} \left| n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x) \right|^q \ dx. \eqno(4.8) $$
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Rosenthal's inequality
nodes.statement: Namely, for arbitrary sequence $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ of independent centered random variables $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot \sqrt{ \sum_{k=1}^n |\zeta_k|_q^2/n }, \hspace{4mm} q \ge 2, \eqno(4.9) $$ where the "Rosenthal's" constant $ K_{R} $ is less than 0.6535, see \cite{Ostrovsky4}. \par If the r.v. $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ are in addition identically distributed, then $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.10) $$

assumptions: for arbitrary sequence $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ of independent centered random variables
conclusions: $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot \sqrt{ \sum_{k=1}^n |\zeta_k|_q^2/n }, \hspace{4mm} q \ge 2, \eqno(4.9) $$
$$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.10) $$
nodes.statement_short: Moment bound for normalized sums of independent centered r.v.s with constant $K_R q/\ln q$, $K_R<0.6535$.

nodes.name: Introduce centered fields
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} Denote $$ \tau_i(x) = f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x) - {\bf E} f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x), \eqno(4.6) $$ $$ S_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x), \eqno(4.7) $$ then $ \tau_i(x) $ is a sequence of independent identical distributed centered random fields which are proportional with coefficient $ 1/\Gamma(1 - \alpha) $ to the considered before r.f. $ \zeta_i(x). $
nodes.statement_short: Introduce centered fields $\tau_i$ and normalized sums $S_n$.
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Fubini-Tonelli
nodes.statement: Let us consider the sequence of random variables $$ V_{\alpha,q}(n) = ||S_n(\cdot)||_q^q = \int_0^1 |S_n(x)|^q \ dx, $$ then we have using Fubini-Tonelli theorem under our condition $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha $ $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) = \int_0^1 {\bf E} |S_n(x)|^q \ dx= \int_0^1 {\bf E} \left| n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \tau_i(x) \right|^q \ dx. \eqno(4.8) $$
nodes.statement_short: Swap expectation and integral in $E\|S_n\|_q^q$.
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Recall Rosenthal's inequality
nodes.statement: We intent to exploit the famous Rosenthal's inequality, see \cite{Rosenthal1}, \cite{Ostrovsky4}. Namely, for arbitrary sequence $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ of independent centered random variables $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot \sqrt{ \sum_{k=1}^n |\zeta_k|_q^2/n }, \hspace{4mm} q \ge 2, \eqno(4.9) $$ where the "Rosenthal's" constant $ K_{R} $ is less than 0.6535, see \cite{Ostrovsky4}. \par If the r.v. $ \{ \zeta_k \} $ are in addition identically distributed, then $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R} \cdot \frac{q}{\ln q} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.10) $$
nodes.statement_short: Recall Rosenthal's inequality with explicit constant.
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Uniform Rosenthal constant
nodes.statement: As long as in this section $ 2 \le q < 1/\alpha, $ $$ \frac{q}{\ln q} \le \max \left[ \frac{2}{\ln 2}, \ \frac{1/\alpha}{|\ln \alpha|} \right], $$ and if we denote $$ K_{R,\alpha} = K_R \cdot \max \left[ \frac{2}{\ln 2}, \ \frac{1/\alpha}{|\ln \alpha|} \right], \eqno(4.11) $$ then there holds the following inequality (under our conditions) $$ \left|\ n^{-1/2} \ \sum_{k=1}^n \zeta_k \ \right|_q \le K_{R,\alpha} \cdot |\zeta_1|_q. \eqno(4.12) $$
nodes.statement_short: Bound $q/\ln q$ uniformly for $2\le q<1/\alpha$, giving constant $K_{R,\alpha}$.
nodes.section: 4 Non-asymptotical error estimation in the Lebesgue-Riesz norm.

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement: We conclude after substitution into (4.8) $$ {\bf E} V_{\alpha,q} (n) \le K(\alpha,q)^q \cdot K^q_{R,\alpha}. \eqno(4.13) $$
nodes.statement_short: Substituting into (4.8) bounds $EV_{\alpha,q}(n)$ by $K(\alpha,q)^qK^q_{R,\alpha}$.

nodes.name: Take q-th root
nodes.statement: It remains to extract the root of degree $ q $ from last inequality to obtain the estimate $$ \sup_n W_{q,n} [ D^{\alpha}[G](\cdot), G_{\alpha,n}(\cdot) ] \le K(\alpha,q) \cdot K_{R,\alpha}, $$ which is equivalent to the assertion if theorem 4.1 with explicit evaluate of constant.
nodes.statement_short: Take q-th root to obtain Theorem 4.1 with explicit constant.

nodes.name: Gaussian stationary sequence, spectral function and spectral density
nodes.statement: Let $ \eta_k, \ k = 1,2,\ldots,n $ be real valued, centered: $ {\bf E} \eta(k) = 0 $ Gaussian distributed stationary random sequence (process) with (unknown) even covariation function $ r = r(m), $ spectral function $ F(\lambda), \ \lambda \in [0, 2 \pi], \ F(0+) = F(0) = 0, $ and with spectral density $ f(\lambda), $ (if there exists): $$ r(m) = \mathop{\rm Cov}\limits(\eta(j+m), \eta(j)) = {\bf E} \eta(j+m)\cdot \eta(j) = $$ $$ \int_{[0, 2 \pi]} \cos(\lambda m) dF(\lambda) = \int_{[0, 2 \pi]} \cos(\lambda m) f(\lambda) \ d \lambda, \eqno(5.1) $$ so that $$ F(\lambda) = \int_0^{\lambda} f(t) dt = I^{(1)}[f](\lambda). $$

nodes.name: Remark 5.2 (uniform confidence bands)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 5.2.} I.A.Ibragimov in \cite{Ibragimov1} proved the asymptotical normality of the random process $ \sqrt{n} \left\{I^1[J_n](\lambda) - I^1[F](\lambda) \right\} $ as $ n \to \infty $ in the space $ C(0, 2 \pi) $ of continuous functions. See also \cite{Dahlhaus1}, \cite{Levit1}. A fortiori, the sequence of random processes $$ \zeta_n(\lambda) = \sqrt{n} \cdot \left\{ F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right\} $$ converges weakly in the space $ C(0, 2 \pi) $ as $ n \to \infty $ to the centered separable Gaussian process $ \zeta_{\infty} $ with covariation function $ \Theta_{\alpha}(\lambda, \mu). $ Therefore $$ {\bf P} \left( \sqrt{n} \cdot \max_{\lambda} \left| \left\{ F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right\} \right| > u \right) \approx {\bf P} (\max_{\lambda} | \zeta_{\infty}(\lambda) | > u), \ u = \mathop{\rm const}\limits > 0. \eqno(5.10) $$ The asymptotical as $ u \to \infty $ behavior of the last probability is fundamental investigated in the monograph \cite{Piterbarg2}, see also \cite{Piterbarg1}: $$ {\bf P} (\max_{\lambda} | \zeta_{\infty}(\lambda) | > u) \sim H(\alpha) \ u^{\kappa - 1} \ \exp \left(-u^2/\sigma^2 \right),\eqno(5.11) $$ $$ H(\alpha), \ \kappa = \mathop{\rm const}\limits, \ \sigma^2 = \sigma^2(\alpha) = \max_{\lambda \in (0, 2 \pi)} \Theta_{\alpha}(\lambda,\lambda). \eqno(5.11a) $$ The last equalities may be used by construction of confidence region for $ F^{(\alpha)}(\cdot) $ in the uniform norm. Indeed, let $ 1 - \delta $ be the reliability of confidence region, for example, $ 0.95 $ or $ 0.99 $ etc. Let $ u_0 = u_0(\delta) $ be a maximal root of the equation $$ H(\alpha) \ u_0^{\kappa - 1} \ \exp \left(-u_0^2/\sigma^2 \right) = \delta, $$ then with probability $ \approx 1 - \delta $ $$ \sup_{\lambda \in (0, 2 \pi)} \left| F_{\alpha,n}(\lambda) - F^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \right| \le \frac{u_0(\delta)}{\sqrt{n}}. \eqno(5.12) $$

nodes.name: Two-dimensional sample
nodes.statement: In detail, let $ \{ (\xi(i), \eta(i)) \}, i = 1,2,\ldots,n $ be a two dimensional non - negative sample with common distribution function.

nodes.name: Bivariate reliability function
nodes.statement: We define the reliability function $ G = G(x,y) $ as follows: $$ G(x,y) = {\bf P}(\xi(i) \ge x, \ \eta(i) > y), \ x,y \ge 0.\eqno(6.1) $$

nodes.name: Mixed Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative
nodes.statement: Let $ \alpha, \beta = \mathop{\rm const}\limits $ be two numbers such that $ 0 < \alpha, \beta < 1; $ (we will suppose further that $ 0 < \alpha, \beta < 1/2.) $ The partial mixed fractional derivative $ D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) $ again of Rieman-Liouville type of order $ (\alpha, \beta) $ of a function $ G(\cdot, \cdot) $ at the positive points $ (x,y) $ is defined as follows: $$ G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) = D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) \stackrel{def}{=} D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [G] = \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \alpha)} \frac{1}{\Gamma(1 - \beta)}\times $$ $$ \frac{\partial^2}{ \partial x \partial y } \int_0^x \int_0^y \frac{G(t,s)\ dt \ ds}{ (x-t)^{\alpha} (y-s)^{\beta} }, \eqno(6.2) $$ see, e.g. \cite{Samko1}, chapter 24.
nodes.statement_short: $G^{(\alpha,\beta)}=D^\alpha_xD^\beta_y[G]$, a mixed second derivative of a double Riemann-Liouville integral.

nodes.name: Convention for nonexistent mixed derivative
nodes.statement: We put as before $ D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) = 0 $ if at the point (in the plane) $ (x,y) $ the expression (4.2) for $ D^{ \alpha, \beta}_{x,y}[G](x,y) $ does not exists.

nodes.name: Mixed fractional derivative of a factorable function
nodes.statement: Note that in general case $ D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] \ne D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H], $ but if the function $ G = G(x,y) $ is factorable: $ H(x,y) = g_1(x) g_2(y) $ and both the functions $ g_x(\cdot) $ and $ g_2(\cdot) $ are "differentiable" at the points $ x $ and $ y $ correspondingly: $$ \exists D^{\alpha}[g_1](x), \hspace{6mm} \exists D^{\beta}[g_2](y), $$ then really $$ D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H] = D^{\alpha}_x[g_1](x) \cdot D^{\beta}_y [g_2](y). \eqno(6.3) $$
assumptions: if the function $ G = G(x,y) $ is factorable: $ H(x,y) = g_1(x) g_2(y) $
conclusions: $$ D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H] = D^{\alpha}_x[g_1](x) \cdot D^{\beta}_y [g_2](y). \eqno(6.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: For factorable $H=g_1g_2$ the mixed fractional derivatives commute and factor.

nodes.name: Factorization of mixed derivative (6.3)
nodes.statement: $$ D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = D^{\beta}_y D^{\alpha}_x [H] = D^{\alpha}_x[g_1](x) \cdot D^{\beta}_y [g_2](y). \eqno(6.3) $$

nodes.name: Bivariate indicator H
nodes.statement: Introduce as a capacity of the function $ H $ the following: $$ H(x,y) := I(\xi \ge x, \ \eta \ge y), \ \xi = \xi(1), \eta = \eta(1). $$

nodes.name: Mixed derivative of the bivariate indicator
nodes.statement: As long as $$ I(\xi \ge x, \ \eta \ge y) = I(\xi \ge x) \cdot I(\eta \ge y), $$ the function $ H = H(x,y) $ is factorable and therefore (see (6.3)) $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta}(y). \eqno(6.4) $$
conclusions: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) D^{\alpha}_x D^{\beta}_y [H] = f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta}(y). \eqno(6.4) $$

nodes.name: Estimate G_{alpha,beta,n} of the mixed fractional derivative
nodes.statement: The consistent with probability one in each fixed point $ (x,y) $ estimate of the function $ G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) $ is follows: $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) G_{\alpha, \beta,n }(x,y) \stackrel{def}{=} n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n f_{\alpha,\xi(i)}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta(i)}(y). \eqno(6.5) $$

nodes.name: Properties of the bivariate estimate
nodes.statement: It is easily to verify that the estimate $ G_{\alpha, \beta,n }(x,y) $ obeys at the same properties as its one-dimensional predecessor $ G_{\alpha, n }(x), $ for example, is unbiased, satisfies LLN and CLT.

nodes.name: Product kernel h_{alpha,beta}
nodes.statement: Note that despite the function $$ h_{\alpha, \beta}(x,y) = h_{\alpha, \beta}(\xi, \eta; x,y) := f_{\alpha,\xi}(x) \cdot f_{\beta,\eta}(y), \ \xi = \xi(1), \eta = \eta(1)\eqno(6.6) $$ is also factorable, we do not suppose the independence of the r.v. $ (\xi, \eta). $

nodes.name: Bivariate normalized random fields S_n(x,y)
nodes.statement: Define as before the following sequence of random fields $$ S_n(x,y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n \left( h_{\alpha, \beta}(\xi(i), \eta(i); x,y) - \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) \right), \eqno(6.7) $$ so that $$ \Gamma(1 - \alpha) \Gamma(1 - \beta) \left[ G_{(\alpha, \beta,n)}(x,y) - G^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x,y) \right] = n^{-1/2} S_n(x,y). \eqno(6.8) $$

nodes.name: Mixed-norm order of h_{alpha,beta}
nodes.statement: Further, it is clear that $$ || h_{\alpha, \beta}(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q,X; r,Y} \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q} \ (1 - \beta r)^{-1/r}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, 1 \le r < 1/\beta. \eqno(6.9) $$
conclusions: $$ || h_{\alpha, \beta}(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q,X; r,Y} \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q} \ (1 - \beta r)^{-1/r}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, 1 \le r < 1/\beta. \eqno(6.9) $$

nodes.name: L_{q,F} norm on the plane
nodes.statement: Let return to the source problem and let us consider only the non-mixed case $ r = q; $ then $$ ||h(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q,q} = ||h(\cdot, \cdot)||_{q, F} = \left[\int_X \int_Y |h(x,y)|^q F(dx,dy) \right]^{1/q}.\eqno(6.10) $$

nodes.name: q >= 2 in the bivariate case
nodes.statement: Assume also $ q \ge 2, $ so $ 2 \le q = r < \min(1/\alpha, 1/\beta). $

nodes.name: Moment growth, case beta < alpha
nodes.statement: {\bf First possibility:} $ \beta < \alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} We find after simple calculations as in fourth section using Rosenthal's inequality: $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_1(\alpha, \beta, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-1}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.11) $$ and $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.11a) $$
conclusions: $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_1(\alpha, \beta, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-1}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.11) $$
$$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.11a) $$
nodes.statement_short: If $\beta<\alpha$: $\sup_n E\|S_n\|^q_{q,F}\asymp(1-\alpha q)^{-1}$ for $q<1/\alpha$, infinite otherwise.

nodes.name: Moment growth, case beta = alpha
nodes.statement: {\bf Second possibility:} $ \beta = \alpha. $ \par \vspace{3mm} We have analogously $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_2(\alpha, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-2}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.12) $$ and $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.12a) $$
conclusions: $$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q \asymp C_2(\alpha, q) \cdot (1 - \alpha q)^{-2}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha, \eqno(6.12) $$
$$ \sup_n {\bf E} || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||_{q,F}^q = \infty, \ q \ge 1/\alpha. \eqno(6.12a) $$
nodes.statement_short: If $\beta=\alpha$: $\sup_n E\|S_n\|^q_{q,F}\asymp(1-\alpha q)^{-2}$ for $q<1/\alpha$, infinite otherwise.

nodes.name: CLT for bivariate fields iff q < 1/alpha
nodes.statement: As a consequence: the sequence of r.f. $ S_n(\cdot, \cdot) $ in both the considered cases satisfies the CLT in the space $ L_q(F(dx, dy)) $ iff $ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $

nodes.name: Bivariate confidence regions
nodes.statement: Thus, there is a possibility to built the asymptotical and non-asymptotical confidence region for estimated mixed fractional derivative $ F^{(\alpha, \beta)}(\cdot, \cdot), \ \alpha, \beta < 1/2 $ still in the multivariate case in the $ L_q(dF) $ norm as well as in the fixed point $ (x_0, y_0). $

nodes.name: Grand Lebesgue Space
nodes.statement: Let $ (X, M, \mu ) $ be a probability space with non-trivial probability measure $ \mu, $ and let also $ \psi = \psi(q), \ 1 \le q < s, \ s = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in (1, \infty] $ be continuous on the open interval $ ( 1, s ) $ bounded from below function. By definition, a Grand Lebesgue Space (GLS) $ G\psi $ over our triplet $ (X, M, \mu ) $ consists on all the measurable functions $ f: X \to R $ with finite norm $$ ||f||G\psi \stackrel{def}{=} \sup_{q \in (1,s)} \left[ \frac{|f|_q}{\psi(q)} \right]. \eqno(7.1) $$
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.
nodes.statement_short: GLS $G\psi$: functions with $\sup_{q}|f|_q/\psi(q)<\infty$.

nodes.name: L_q norm and support of psi
nodes.statement: Hereafter $$ |f|_q = \left[ \int_X |f(x)|^q \ \mu(dx) \right]^{1/q} $$ and we will denote $ s = \mathop{\rm supp}\limits \psi. $
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Product measure mu on [0,1] x Omega
nodes.statement: We choose supposing without loss of generality $ a = 0, \ b = 1, $ so that $ \dim \xi = 1 $ and $ F(0+) = 0, \ F(1 - 0) = 1, \ F \in K, \ \alpha \in (0,1/2), $ $$ X = [0,1] \otimes \Omega, $$ so that the measure $ \mu $ is direct product of ordinary Lebesgue measure $ dx $ and probability measure $ P: $ $$ \mu(A \otimes B) = \int_A dx \cdot {\bf P}(B), \ A \subset [0,1], \ B \subset \Omega, \eqno(7.2) $$ where $ \Omega = \{ \omega \} $ is source probability space, i.e. in which is defined our sample $ \{ \xi(i) \}. $
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Proposition 7.1 (tail estimate)
nodes.statement: {\bf Proposition 7.1.} $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,\omega): |S_n(x)| > u \} \le C_3(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.3) $$
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.
conclusions: $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,\omega): |S_n(x)| > u \} \le C_3(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.3) $$
nodes.statement_short: Uniformly in n, the $\mu$-measure of $\{|S_n|>u\}$ is $O(u^{-\alpha}\ln u)$.

nodes.name: Tail estimate (7.3)
nodes.statement: $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,\omega): |S_n(x)| > u \} \le C_3(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.3) $$
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.1
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} Put $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) = (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$ Note that $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-\alpha}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$ The assertion (4.5) may be rewritten as follows. $$ \sup_n | S_n(\cdot, \cdot) |_{q, \mu} \le C_4(\alpha) \ \psi_{\alpha}(q), \eqno(7.4) $$ or equally on the language of the Grand Lebesgue Spaces $$ \sup_n || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||G\psi_{\alpha} \le C_4(\alpha) < \infty. \eqno(7.5) $$ The tail estimate (7.3) follows immediately from one of results of the article \cite{Ostrovsky7}; see also \cite{Ostrovsky8}.
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite Theorem 4.1 as a bound in the Grand Lebesgue Space $G\psi_\alpha$ and convert to a tail estimate by a GLS tail result.

nodes.name: Define psi_alpha
nodes.statement: {\bf Proof.} Put $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) = (1 - \alpha q)^{-1/q}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$ Note that $$ \psi_{\alpha}(q) \asymp (1 - \alpha q)^{-\alpha}, \ 1 \le q < 1/\alpha. $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\psi_\alpha(q)=(1-\alpha q)^{-1/q}$.
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Rewrite Theorem 4.1 in GLS
nodes.statement: The assertion (4.5) may be rewritten as follows. $$ \sup_n | S_n(\cdot, \cdot) |_{q, \mu} \le C_4(\alpha) \ \psi_{\alpha}(q), \eqno(7.4) $$ or equally on the language of the Grand Lebesgue Spaces $$ \sup_n || S_n(\cdot, \cdot) ||G\psi_{\alpha} \le C_4(\alpha) < \infty. \eqno(7.5) $$
nodes.statement_short: (4.5) says $\sup_n\|S_n\|_{G\psi_\alpha}<\infty$.
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: GLS tail estimate
nodes.statement: The tail estimate (7.3) follows immediately from one of results of the article \cite{Ostrovsky7}; see also \cite{Ostrovsky8}.
nodes.statement_short: GLS norm bound implies the tail bound (Ostrovsky-Sirota).
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.

nodes.name: Remark 7.1 (bivariate tail estimates)
nodes.statement: {\bf Remark 7.1.} It is not hard to generalize this result into the multidimensional case described in the $ 6^{th} $ section. Namely, if in the notations of the $ 6^{th} $ section $ 0 < \beta < \alpha < 1/2, $ then $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,y, \omega): |S_n(x,y)| > u \} \le C_5(\alpha, \beta) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln u, \ u \ge e; \eqno(7.6) $$ if $ 0 < \beta = \alpha < 1/2, $ then $$ \sup_n \mu \{ (x,y, \omega): |S_n(x,y)| > u \} \le C_6(\alpha) \ u^{-\alpha} \ \ln^2 u, \ u \ge e. \eqno(7.7) $$
nodes.section: 7 Estimation of fractional derivative in Grand Lebesgue Space norm.
nodes.statement_short: In the bivariate case the tail bound is $u^{-\alpha}\ln u$ if $\beta<\alpha$ and $u^{-\alpha}\ln^2u$ if $\beta=\alpha$.

nodes.name: Weighted fractional derivative estimation
nodes.statement: Perhaps, it is interest to investigate the error of the approximation of a form $$ V(x) \cdot ( W \cdot F)^{(\alpha)}(x) \approx V(x) \cdot ( W \cdot F)_{n,\alpha}(x), $$ or analogously $$ V(x) \cdot ( W * F)^{(\alpha)}(x) \approx V(x) \cdot ( W * F)_{n,\alpha}(x), $$ or analogously $$ V(x) * ( W * F)^{(\alpha)}(x) \approx V(x) *( W * F)_{n,\alpha}(x), $$ where $ V(x), W(x) $ are two weight functions, for instance, $ V(x) = |x|^{\gamma}, \ W(x) = |x|^{\Delta}, \hspace{6mm} \gamma, \Delta = \mathop{\rm const}\limits. $

nodes.name: Parametric family sample
nodes.statement: Let $ \xi(i), \ i = 1,2,\ldots,n $ be a sample of a volume $ n $ with parametric family of regular distribution of a form $$ {\bf P} (\xi(i) < x) = F(x; \theta), $$ where $ \theta \in \Theta \subset R^k, \ k < \infty $ is (multidimensional, in general case) unknown numerical parameter.

nodes.name: Maximum likelihood estimate
nodes.statement: Denote by $ \hat{\theta}_n $ the maximum likelihood estimate of the parameter $ \theta $ builded on our sample.

nodes.name: Semi-parametric goodness-of-fit statistic tau_n
nodes.statement: The asymptotical tail behavior of distribution for the following statistic $$ \tau_n := \sqrt{n} \cdot || F(\cdot, \hat{\theta}_n ) - F_n(\cdot) ||L, $$ where $ || \cdot||L $ is some Banach functional norm in the space $ x \in R, $ is in detail investigated in \cite{Piterbarg1}, \cite{Piterbarg2}, chapter 5.

nodes.name: Tail behavior of the fractional semi-parametric statistic
nodes.statement: By our opinion, it is interest to obtain also the asymptotical tail behavior of the following statistic $$ \tau_{n,\alpha} := \sqrt{n} \cdot || F^{(\alpha)}(\cdot, \hat{\theta}_n ) - F_{n,\alpha}(\cdot) ||L, $$ $ \alpha = \mathop{\rm const}\limits \in (0, 1/2). $

nodes.name: Possible statistical applications
nodes.statement: The asymptotical tail behavior of the statistic $ \tau_{n,\alpha} $ may be used perhaps in turn in statistics, for instance, for the verification of semi-parametrical hypotheses and detection of distortion times etc.
